How to read this

Every camp below carries two numbers from the Forest Service list: how many people it holds at low water and how many at high water. They are often different, and that difference is the most useful thing on this page. 45 of the 92 camps are beaches that do not exist at high water. 4 more shrink. One exists only at high water.

The capacities are limits, not suggestions. A group may not use a camp that is rated for fewer people than it has, so a party of 12 cannot take a 10-person beach, reserved or not.

The list does not say what flow separates low from high. Treat the June runoff as high water and expect the low-water beaches to come out as the river drops through July. If you launch early, or the year is a big one, plan on the high-water numbers and check today’s flow before you fill in a request.

Requesting reserved camps

The Forest Service now assigns reservable camps ahead of time, by email, not at the Corn Creek launch. For launches from June 15 through September 7 the River Office emails the permit holder a camp request form 14 days before the launch date.

  • Submit the form at least 7 days before launch. It can be submitted once. Miss it and you get no reservable camps.
  • A permit can hold at most 5 reservable camps.
  • Groups of fewer than 21 on a 7- or 8-day trip may not reserve large camps. On a trip of 6 days or fewer they may ask, but groups of 21 or more are assigned large camps first.
  • No layovers in a reservable camp, and you must be in the camp on the date printed on the permit.
  • Be in a reserved camp by 7 PM Mountain time and out by noon. After 7 PM an empty reservable camp is open to anyone.
  • Reserved camps are final once the permit is issued, which happens by email 5 or 6 days before launch.
  • Everything not marked reservable is first-come.

Trip length follows group size during the control season: up to 8 days for 1–10 people, 7 days for 11–20, and 6 days for 21–30. Rules change; the Salmon-Challis National Forest page is the authority, and this summary was checked against it on 2026-09-30.

Picking camps for your group

Groups of 21 to 30
Only the 30-person camps are open to you: 44 at low water, 33 at high. Large reservable camps that hold 30 at any level: Lower Devil's Teeth 13, Blackadar Hole 17, Barth Camp 23.1, Lower Yellowpine 36.8, Big Mallard 36.9, Groundhog Bar 44, Rhett Creek 46.6, Haynie Bar 53.4, Mackay Bar Bridge 55.4, Mann Creek 60.6, Warren Creek 61, Swimming Hole 61.6.
Groups of 10 or fewer
23 camps are capped at 10 people, so no larger group can take them. The reservable ones: Ruff Creek 43.2, Teepee Creek 51.2.
Early-season and high-water trips
Plan around the 47 camps with a high-water capacity. First-come camps that hold 30 at high water: Upper Horse Creek 3.4, Lower Horse Creek 3.5, Little Squaw Creek 10.7, Lower Lantz Bar 11.1, Tag Creek 11.3, Disappointment Creek 11.7, Elkhorn Creek 14.7, Upper Corey Bar 19.6, Sunny Bar 22.6, Hotsprings Camp 22.8, Poor Bar 24.2, Magpie 29.5, Bargamin 32, Upper Yellowpine 36.7, Boiler Hole 38.3, Pebble Beach 53.2, Bluebird Hole 53.7, Deadman's Hole 55.7, South Fork 56.5, Lower Bull Creek 69.3, Upper Sheep Creek 73.9.
Hot-weather trips
Camps a source describes as shaded: Lunch Bar 2.5, Upper Horse Creek 3.4, Otter Beach 10, Fawn Creek 10.2, Little Squaw Creek 10.7, Tag Creek 11.3, Blackadar Hole 17, Sunny Bar 22.6, Boiler Hole 38.3, Gaines Bar 46.3, Five Mile Creek 52.6, Pebble Beach 53.2, Bluebird Hole 53.7, Hungry Bar 60.3, Indian Creek Bar 62.2, James Creek 62.4, Alex Meadows 67.2, Lower Sheep Creek 74.1, Slide Beach 75.2. Described as exposed or hot: Rhett Creek 46.6, No Man Beach 51, Mackay Bar Bridge 55.4, South Fork Island 56.7, Basin Creek 67.8, Upper Bull Creek 69.1, Maxwell Bar 72.8, Upper Sheep Creek 73.9.
Kids, new boaters, tired crews
Easy landings: Legend Creek 4.7, Black Canyon Beach 21.4, Paine Creek 49, No Man Beach 51, Five Mile Creek 52.6, Bluebird Hole 53.7, Cove Creek 57.8, Middle Sheep 74. Maxwell Bar 72.8 has a sand dune to jump from. Landings that need attention: Lower Horse Creek 3.5, Upper Lantz Bar 10.6, Little Squaw Creek 10.7, Upper Devil's Teeth 12.9, Motor 17.2, Lower Corey Bar 19.7, Sunny Bar 22.6, Barth Camp 23.1, Bruin Bar 24.8, Hancock 25.9, Groundhog Bar 44, Gaines Bar 46.3, Haynie Bar 53.4, South Fork 56.5, South Fork Island 56.7, Mann Creek 60.6, Warren Creek 61.
Hot springs
Camps at the Barth hot springs: Sunny Bar 22.6, Hotsprings Camp 22.8, Barth Camp 23.1.
History and rock art
Pictographs: Legend Creek 4.7, Lower Devil's Teeth 13. Homesteads, graves and relics: Spindle Creek 6.1, Blackadar Hole 17, Motor 17.2, Big Squaw Creek 17.9, Barth Camp 23.1, Upper Yellowpine 36.7, Oakie Groggs 37.5, Boiler Hole 38.3, Jim Moore 42.8, Gaines Bar 46.3, Teepee Creek 51.2, Five Mile Creek 52.6, Red Harland Hole 58.1, Rabbit Creek 65.2.
Hikers
Chamberlin Creek 15.4, Bargamin 32, Upper Yellowpine 36.7, Reed Creek 45.2, Paine Creek 49, Warren Creek 61, Indian Creek Bar 62.2, Lower Bull Creek 69.3.
If you want quiet
These have planes, jet boats, vehicles or day visitors nearby: Upper Allison Campsite 33.4, Allison Ranch Campsite 33.5, Jim Moore 42.8, Wilson Bar 54.1, Mackay Bar Bridge 55.4, Deadman's Hole 55.7.

The aerials, and the photos still missing

Every camp has an aerial from the USDA’s National Agriculture Imagery Program, which is public domain. These were flown between 21 Sep 2021 and 30 Sep 2021, with the river at 2,790–2,900 cfs at White Bird: very low water, so they show the beaches at close to their largest. Each frame is 1.2 km across with north at the top. The Forest Service publishes river miles, not coordinates, so a frame is centred on the camp’s mile along the river’s mapped centerline, which is good to about a quarter mile: the camp is in the picture, near the middle, on the bank the entry names.

What an aerial cannot show is the camp from the boat, or the same beach at high water. Nobody publishes ground photos of these camps that can be reused, so each entry has room for a low-water and a high-water photograph, and they are empty.

Send one in. If you have a photo of a named camp, email it to owen@lateboof.com with the camp name, the date, and the flow if you know it. The same camp at two different levels is the most useful thing you can send. Corrections to anything on this page go to the same address.

Sources and what this is not

Mile, river side, both capacities, reservable status and the quoted note on every camp come from the Forest Service, Wild Main Salmon Campsites (2025). Camp names are spelled as that list spells them, because that is what the request form uses. The descriptions are LateBoof’s own wording; details beyond the Forest Service list were checked against GoRafting, Main Salmon River Rafting Guide, and where the two disagree the Forest Service figure is used and the camp says so.

Nothing here comes from a LateBoof trip yet. Beaches move, creeks blow out, and camps burn; a description is a starting point for a conversation with someone who was there last season, not a promise. Checked 2026-09-30.
